questions.stem: A client with acute kidney injury has a potassium level of 6.8 milliequivalents per liter and peaked T waves on the ECG. Which prescription should the nurse implement first?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Polystyrene sulfonate removes potassium over hours; it does not protect the heart from an immediate dysrhythmia.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Calcium gluconate stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes, protecting against lethal dysrhythmias while other measures lower the potassium.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Dietary restriction is important long term but does nothing for an acute, life-threatening potassium level with ECG changes.

questions.teachingPoint: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes: give calcium first to protect the heart, then insulin with glucose to shift potassium, then remove it.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes has deep, rapid respirations, a fruity breath odor, a blood glucose of 480 milligrams per deciliter and an arterial pH of 7.22. Which initial intervention should the nurse anticipate?

options.label: A
options.text: An intravenous bolus of regular insulin before any fluids
options.rationale: Insulin is essential but is started after fluid resuscitation and once potassium is known, because it drives potassium into cells.

options.label: B
options.text: An infusion of 0.9 percent sodium chloride
options.rationale: Diabetic ketoacidosis causes profound dehydration; isotonic fluid restores perfusion and is the first step before insulin.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is reserved for severe acidosis with pH below 6.9 and is not a routine first intervention.

questions.teachingPoint: Diabetic ketoacidosis management: fluids first, then insulin infusion with potassium monitoring, then glucose-containing fluids as glucose falls.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure reports gaining three pounds in two days and being short of breath when lying flat. Which is the nurse's best interpretation of these findings?

options.label: A
options.text: An expected effect of the client's diuretic therapy
options.rationale: Diuretics should produce weight loss; rapid gain means fluid is being retained despite treatment.

options.label: B
options.text: Fluid volume overload that should be reported to the provider
options.rationale: A gain of more than two to three pounds in a few days with orthopnea indicates worsening heart failure and needs prompt treatment adjustment.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Dehydration would cause weight loss and would not produce orthopnea.

questions.teachingPoint: Teach clients with heart failure to weigh daily and report a gain of two to three pounds in a day or five pounds in a week.
